scenes.name: Vietnam llega a casa
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: 1966 fue el año en que Vietnam golpeó de lleno a Estados Unidos: de 185.000 soldados en enero a 385.000 en diciembre, el mayor aumento de toda la guerra. Era una guerra de adolescentes (edad media de diecinueve años) que reabrió la brecha generacional: Abraham sacrificando a Isaac. El sistema de reclutamiento, en manos de juntas de hombres blancos mayores con pasado militar, favorecía a los privilegiados (los universitarios eran el 2 % de los reclutas); el 80 % de los que sirvieron venían de familias obreras o pobres y los negros eran el 31 % de las tropas de combate. El SNCC condenó la guerra el 6 de enero de 1966 y Muhammad Ali, reclasificado I-A en febrero, dijo que no tenía nada contra el Vietcong. «The Ballad of the Green Berets» del sargento Barry Sadler, boina verde herido en Vietnam, fue número 1 cinco semanas desde el 5 de marzo y el mayor éxito del año: propaganda eficaz, monolítica, sin ambigüedad. Ayudó a que la aprobación de Johnson subiera al 67 % en abril, su techo; en Reino Unido, sin reclutamiento ni tropas en Vietnam, Jagger y los Beatles la llamaron enferma y propaganda. «Greetings (This Is Uncle Sam)» de los Monitors fue de los primeros discos que contaron la experiencia negra del reclutamiento.

scenes.name: De los derechos civiles al Black Power
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: «No se puede hablar del funk sin hablar de la Revolución Negra» (Shock G). Las sentadas, los Freedom Rides y la Marcha sobre Washington de 1963 llevaron el gospel a la calle («A Change Is Gonna Come», «Keep on Pushing»), pero pese a las leyes la masa negra apenas notó cambios. Malcolm X habló por los desposeídos y su asesinato en 1965 dejó un vacío: «It was a funky deal» (Etheridge Knight). Vinieron Watts (con el DJ Magnificent Montague pinchando «Burn, Baby, Burn»), el grito de «Black Power» en la marcha de Meredith de 1966, el SNCC sin blancos, los Panteras Negras de Huey Newton y Bobby Seale en Oakland (armados en el Capitolio de California en 1967, «la mayor amenaza» para Hoover), Newark y Detroit en 1967, los disturbios tras el asesinato de King en 1968, los puños de Tommie Smith y John Carlos en México y el «ningún Vietcong me llamó nigger» de Muhammad Ali. Futuros músicos funk (Marshall Jones de los Ohio Players, Bootsy en Cincinnati, Mudbone Cooper en Baltimore) tiraron piedras en los disturbios: la universidad de la calle. «Say It Loud – I’m Black and I’m Proud» de James Brown convirtió «black» en elogio; «Black Is Beautiful» invirtió siglos de lenguaje y hasta «funky» se reivindicó. Esa libertad de redefinir lo negro fue la incubadora del funk.

podcast.title: Early Life & Ambition (1963)
podcast.body: Born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, he was interviewed for a Time magazine cover story at 21 years old in 1963. He expressed grand ambitions for his future, including driving down Walnut Street on Derby Day and being recognized as an Olympic champion and aspiring heavyweight champion. "I'm going to drive down Walnut Street in a caddy on Derby Day. And all the people will point and say, there goes Cashus Clay."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Conversion to Islam & Name Change (1964)
podcast.body: Six months after his victory over Sonny Liston, Cassius Clay announced he had converted to Islam and changed his name to Muhammad Ali, a decision met with significant speculation and suspicion. "Cashus Clay announced that he was a Muslim and his name was now Muhammad Ali."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Victory over Sonny Liston (1964)
podcast.body: Ali, then Cassius Clay, defeated Sonny Liston on February 25, 1964, in Miami. Liston was widely considered one of the toughest and meanest fighters in boxing history and was managed by the mafia. "Clay did beat Sonny Liston, who by all accounts is one of the toughest meanest fighters ever to step in the ring."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Draft Resistance & Conviction (1965-1970)
podcast.body: Ali initially failed his United States Army induction test due to low writing and spelling scores, but his draft status was revised in November 1965. Citing his opposition to the Vietnam War, Ali refused induction at the Houston induction center, stating, "I will not go if draft it." He was subsequently charged and convicted of draft evasion, stripped of his heavyweight title and boxing license for three years, and faced five years in prison. "He was eventually charged and convicted of draft evasion. He was stripped of his heavyweight title. He was stripped of his licensed box for the next three years and he was facing five years in prison."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Liston Rematch & Controversy (1965)
podcast.body: Ali beat Sonny Liston again in a rematch in May 1965, held in Lewiston, Maine. This unusual location for such a high-profile fight was chosen because very few cities wanted to host Ali or his fights following his announcement of converting to Islam. "In May 1965, Ali beat Liston in a rematch in Lewis and Maine of all places."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Dick Cavett Show Appearance (1970)
podcast.body: On May 25, 1970, Ali appeared on The Dick Cavett Show, where he famously articulated his reasons for draft resistance. When asked about going to jail, he connected his personal sacrifice to the broader struggle of black people, stating, "So why should I worry about going to a little old jail to free my poor people who've been catching hell here for 400 years?" This statement received significant applause from the studio audience. "So why should I worry about going to a little old jail to free my poor people who've been catching hell here for 400 years?"

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Jerry Quarry Fights (1970, 1972)
podcast.body: Ali's return to the ring on October 26, 1970, saw him defeat Jerry Quarry by technical knockout. He later won a rematch against Quarry in 1972 in Las Vegas. "The fight between Ali and Jerry Quarry was on for October 26th. Ali won it on a technical knockout and the same for the rematch in 1972 in Las Vegas."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Return to Boxing (1970)
podcast.body: In September 1970, a federal judge restored Ali's right to fight, ending his three-year boxing ban. Despite California Governor Ronald Reagan's refusal to allow a "draft Dodger" to box in his state and similar opposition from Georgia's governor, a fight was approved in Atlanta by its mayor. "In September 1970, a federal judge restored Ali's right to fight."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Loss to Ken Norton (1973)
podcast.body: On March 31, 1973, Ali suffered only his second career loss to Ken Norton, during which Norton also broke Ali's jaw. "including a match in which he lost to Ken Norton, only the second loss of his career, and Norton also broke his job. That was March 31st, 1973."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Mobutu's Favor (1974)
podcast.body: For the Rumble in the Jungle, Muhammad Ali received $5 million to fight in Zaire and was flown to the country on President Mobutu's personal plane, highlighting the preferential treatment he received from the Zairian dictator. "They didn't get to fly into Zaire on Mobutu's personal plane the way Ali did."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Overloaded Flight to Zaire (1974)
podcast.body: Ali's plane journey to Zaire was so heavily laden with James Brown's musical equipment that it "barely made it off the ground," illustrating the significant logistical challenges and the volume of gear transported for the music festival. "Ali crammed onto a plane that was so overloaded with James Brown's gear that the plane barely made it off the ground."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Rumble in the Jungle Victory (1974)
podcast.body: In the iconic Rumble in the Jungle fight in Zaire, Muhammad Ali knocked out George Foreman in the eighth round, reclaiming the heavyweight championship of the world in 1974. This victory, timed for US television, cemented his comeback as an underdog and further solidified his status as potentially "the most famous black man in the world." "Muhammad Ali knocked out George Foreman in the eighth round and reclaimed the heavyweight championship of the world."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Underdog Status for Rumble in the Jungle (1974)
podcast.body: At 32 years old, Ali was widely regarded as a significant underdog against the heavyweight champion George Foreman for the Rumble in the Jungle. This perception helped transform him from a controversial figure into a national treasure, with even his corner man, boxing legend Archie Moore, expressing fears that Foreman might kill Ali. "And you would have been hard pressed to find anyone who believed that Muhammad Ali at the age of 32 could beat the heavyweight champion, George Foreman."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Victory over Joe Frazier (1974)
podcast.body: In January 1974, Ali defeated Joe Frazier, a pivotal win that positioned him for a shot at the heavyweight title. "Ali beat Joe Frazier in January 1974, he had his eye on the heavyweight title."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Boxing Champ and Provocateur
podcast.body: Known as Cassius Clay before becoming Muhammad Ali, he was a boxing champion and a provocateur. In 1963, he ventured into music, releasing an album where he engaged in "the dozens" in a proto-rap style, openly dissing his boxing rivals. "Ever the provocateur in 1963, while still known as Cacheus Clay, he released an album called What Else I Am the Greatest, that spent nearly half a year on the Billboard LP's chart, reaching number 61."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Calling Sam Cooke a Rock and Roll Singer
podcast.body: Muhammad Ali famously referred to Sam Cooke as "the greatest rock and roll singer in the world," a classification that was unchallenged at the time, highlighting how music now labeled as soul was then considered rock and roll. "So for example, this footage of Muhammad Ali calling Sam Cook, the greatest rock and roll singer in the world, and at the time absolutely nobody would have questioned Cook being called rock and roll, but these days he would only be talked about as a soul singer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Divisive Figure (1970s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, Muhammad Ali was an incredibly divisive figure in America. Many people "simply hated him" and would watch his fights hoping he would lose, a sharp contrast to his later image, such as lighting the Olympic torch in Atlanta in 1996 while suffering from Parkinson's disease. "A lot of people simply hated him and watched his fights just hoping he would lose."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Later Career & Retirement
podcast.body: Ali later lost and subsequently reclaimed the heavyweight title a third time in fights against Leon Spinks. These later fights occurred "long after he probably should have retired to preserve his health," despite his continued ability to compete at an elite level. "He would lose it again and reclaim it at third time, both in fights to Leon Spanx long after he probably should have retired to preserve his health."
